                                       PROJECT NO. 58777
 TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                            §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                         §
                                                                        OF TEXAS
 REGION UNDER §25.508                             §


               TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ COMMENTS

                                       I.   INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates Commission Staff’s (Staff’s)

careful deliberation on the appropriate assumptions for the Reliability Assessment. The results

from the assessment will be an important barometer for the continued success of the ERCOT

market and whether any market design changes are needed. Choices that are made regarding the

underlying data and how it is weighted will drive the results of the study. Giving undue weight to

extremely unlikely scenarios will drive unachievable goals and make the system appear less

reliable than it actually is. Similarly, overstated load forecasts will predict reliability issues that

are unlikely to materialize. TIEC encourages the Commission to be measured and reasonable in

selecting the appropriate parameters to avoid overstating actual risks or driving uneconomic

market design changes. Ultimately, the Reliability Assessment should be used to inform decisions

about long-term market design and incentives, recognizing that it is not realistic to expect

meaningful changes by 2029 based on changes made in 2026. This is particularly true in light of

current supply chain issues for new gas generation.

       TIEC is highly concerned about basing a Reliability Assessment on current load forecasts

when ERCOT, policymakers, and the market are still trying to implement Senate Bill (SB) 6 and

rationalize these unprecedented large load projections. The surge in potential large loads has

caused issues in processing interconnection requests and transmission planning, making it unclear

how many large loads will actually materialize and on what timeline.               The loads in the


                                                  1
 interconnection queue will go through a novel batching process, likely requiring additional

transmission upgrades on an unknown timeline. It remains unseen which of these large loads will

be able to satisfy the pending criteria in Project No. 58480 and 58481. As a result, it is highly

likely that only a fraction of the loads currently seeking interconnection will actually energize by

2029. TIEC believes it would be rash and premature to make major market design changes

premised on these highly uncertain load forecasts. Understanding the proper load and generation

forecast is critical for the Reliability Assessment because every subsequent market and planning

decision flows from those initial assumptions. The market cannot respond to information it has

not received. Generators and developers need clear signals about the amount and timing of load

growth before they can make multi-year investment commitments.                    Until the Commission

establishes confidence in the load forecast through the criteria approved in Project No. 58480 and

finalizing the large load interconnection process, the market will continue to face uncertainty that

prevents efficient resource development. Making major market overhauls or resource adequacy

determinations based on uncertain forecasts risks creating solutions for problems that may not

materialize.

        As described in more detail below, ERCOT is pancaking several layers of conservative

planning assumptions that will almost certainly lead to unrealistic projections: excessive load

forecasts, understated generation forecasts, a restrictive magnitude threshold, undue weighting of

low-probability weather years, discounting weatherization impacts, and potentially double-

counting outages. This approach is consistent with ERCOT’s tendency (and strong incentive) to

present overly conservative short-term and long-term forecasts following Winter Storm Uri. 1

        To ensure the accuracy of ERCOT’s data, TIEC requests that ERCOT provide full

transparency regarding its load and generation forecast assumptions and methodologies for

stakeholder feedback before finalizing the inputs for the 2026 Reliability Assessment.

Specifically, ERCOT should make available detailed data sets— with hourly demand profiles for

all of the weather years included in the analysis so as to enable stakeholders to review and validate

the forecasting approach. This transparency is essential to create market trust and necessary for

stakeholders to provide accurate feedback on ERCOT’s assumptions. If these results once again

indicate that Winter Storm Uri is driving the results, this will inform the Commission of what

actions, if any, should be taken.


                                        II.    COMMENTS

(1)     At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
        $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the
        triennial reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has
        proposed a plan for updating this CONE value.

        a.     Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment?
               Why or why not?
        b.     If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of
               tasks proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026
               filing an acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide
               recommended modifications to their approach.
        The current CONE was adopted two years ago, and TIEC does not think it is prudent to

materially change this estimate based on short-term supply chain issues. CONE is an estimate of

the present, annualized capital cost (net of energy and ancillary service margins) to build a

generation facility using a reference technology that is the most likely “entry point” for the market.

Typically, CONE is based on the technology with the lowest Net-CONE, i.e., the annualized

                                                  4
 capital carrying cost net of energy and ancillary service margin. This value is then used in planning

studies to determine whether the market design delivers effective price signals to encourage

investment. The results of the planning analyses are for informational purposes, and do not

actually indicate whether resources will invest in the market or whether they will ultimately build

the reference technology. For example, in 2024, WattBridge invested in refurbished LM6000

turbines (at an undisclosed capital cost) because WattBridge believed they had a cost advantage

over the type of plant used for CONE estimates. 5                Developers will conduct independent

calculations of potential revenues to identify the technology that will allow them to recoup their

investment and make a profit. The reference technology for CONE should still be the expected

most economic entry point.

        The driving impediment to generation development in ERCOT today is not achieving

CONE but navigating short-term supply chain constraints. During the recent ERCOT CONE

workshop, Brattle suggested that the current CONE value should be updated because of changes

in the market related to surging demand, supply chain issues, and higher prices. 6 However, these

are temporary issues, and it does not make sense to treat the short-term problems as the economic

equilibrium for the 2026 and 2029 compliance evaluations.

        For these reasons, a holistic change to the reference technology, CONE model, and bottom-

up cost analyses, as Brattle suggests, is inappropriate. The value of CONE should be based on the

long-term viability of a resource, and it is not clear that the viability of Frame CTs has changed

since 2024. Further, updating CONE as outlined in Brattle’s proposal or front-end loading the

(2)    ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in
       this study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP
       compliance plan described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480.
       ERCOT acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance
       plan could be ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the
       reliability assessment by at least a month.

       a.      Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026
               reliability assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in
               Project No. 58480, even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?
       b.      What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load
               forecast used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?
       The forecast used for the Reliability Assessment should incorporate the Senate Bill (SB) 6

eligibility criteria for large loads to the extent feasible, as well as other appropriate adjustments to

reflect the different purpose of the load forecasts.        Specifically, different assumptions and

modeling techniques are required for a resource adequacy forecast as compared to a transmission

planning forecast.

       As discussed in previous rulemakings, the boom in data center/computing loads, third-

party developer interconnection activities, and existing growth in the ERCOT region have made

forecasting increasingly difficult and uncertain. SB 6 and Project Nos. 58480 and 58481 aim to

reduce some of the uncertainty by establishing criteria to validate large loads. Even though using

the process approved in PUC Subst. R. § 25.370 could create some delays, having more accurate



                                                   7
 load data would produce a more realistic Reliability Assessment. In fact, additional adjustments

to the forecast may be necessary to provide an accurate baseline.

        First, the data provided by DSPs under the compliance plan approved in Project No. 58480

should be adjusted because it is being used in a resource adequacy analysis, not for transmission

planning. As the Commission explained when approving the language in PUC Subst. R. §

25.370(e)(3), there should be adjustments in the underlying assumptions or methodologies used to

develop a forecast based on how it will be used. 10 Unlike a transmission planning forecast,

resource adequacy studies are not used as an initial screening tool and they are not subject to

ongoing refinements as loads update their plans and decide not to move forward. Some discount

for execution risk should be applied for resource adequacy, even though this may not be

appropriate for transmission planning.

        Second, the purpose of a resource adequacy forecast is to predict the most likely

situations—e.g. expected demand given a weather year—because the goal is to define the amount

and quantity of excess reserves that are needed to handle contingencies and achieve certain

reliability goals. Conversely, a transmission planning analysis must incorporate extreme, low

probability demand levels in a subregion of ERCOT in the forecast itself, because there is no

reserve margin and the system must be built to withstand reasonably likely contingencies. For

example, it is not realistic to assume that each subregion will reach its individual non-coincident

peak at the same time. Historical evidence does not support this, so summing the individual non-

coincident demands for each subregion from the transmission forecast in a resource adequacy

analysis would therefore be fundamentally incorrect. It would also undoubtedly lead to unrealistic

        Third, the load forecast should be adjusted to be consistent with ERCOT’s expectations for

transmission development and the batch study process. Importantly, the Reliability Assessment

does not occur in a vacuum, and policy decisions around the interconnection and energization of

large loads will materially impact the load forecast. For instance, the DSP load forecast data likely

before they can interconnect. ERCOT has indicated that transmission lines take about 6 years to

build, 11 so any load that is dependent on this type of long-lead time infrastructure will not be able

to energize until after 2029. As such, the planning assumptions should be careful not to presume

near‑term service for loads requiring major “greenfield” transmission upgrades.               Similarly,

However, TIEC recommends several additional adjustments to reflect realistic resource additions

and retirements.

       As discussed in previous rulemakings, the boom in data center/computing loads, third-

party developer interconnection activities, and existing growth in the ERCOT region have made

forecasting increasingly difficult and uncertain. SB 6 and Project Nos. 58480 and 58481 aim to

        First, the data provided by DSPs under the compliance plan approved in Project No. 58480

should be adjusted because it is being used in a resource adequacy analysis, not for transmission

planning.    As the Commission explained when approving the language in PUC Subst. R. §

25.370(e)(3), there should be adjustments in the underlying assumptions or methodologies used to

develop a forecast based on how it will be used. 10 Unlike a transmission planning forecast,

resource adequacy studies are not used as an initial screening tool and they are not subj ect to

ongoing refinements as loads update their plans and decide not to move forward. Some discount

for execution risk should be applied for resource adequacy, even though this may not be

appropriate for transmission planning.

        Second, the purpose of a resource adequacy forecast is to predict the most likely

situations-e. g expected demand given a weather year-because the goal is to define the amount

and quantity of excess reserves that are needed to handle contingencies and achieve certain

reliability goals . Conversely , a transmission planning analysis must incorporate extreme, low

probability demand levels in a subregion of ERCOT in the forecast itself, because there is no

reserve margin and the system must be built to withstand reasonably likely contingencies. For

example, it is not realistic to assume that each subregion will reach its individual non-coincident

peak at the same time. Historical evidence does not support this, so summing the individual non-

coincident demands for each subregion from the transmission forecast in a resource adequacy

analysis would therefore be fundamentally incorrect. It would also undoubtedly lead to unrealistic

    TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS' EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 To ensure the accuracy of ERCOT' s data, TIEC requests that ERCOT provide full
 transparency regarding its load and generation forecast assumptions and methodologies for
 stakeholder feedback before finalizing the inputs for the 2026 Reliability Assessment.
 Specifically, ERCOT should make available detailed data sets- with hourly demand profiles
 for all of the weather years included in the analysis so as to enable stakeholders to review and
 validate the forecasting approach.
 ERCOT's current methodology pancakes several layers of conservative planning assumptions
 that will almost certainly lead to unrealistic projections: excessive load forecasts, understated
 generation forecasts, a restrictive magnitude threshold, undue weighting of low-probability
 weather years, discounting weatherization impacts, and potentially double-counting outages.
 ERCOT's raw analysis should not be used to make major market design changes that could
 result in billions of dollars in wealth transfers with limited or no incremental reliability
 benefits.
 CONE was adopted based on the long-term viability of a resource, and it is not clear that short-
 term supply chain issues have changed the viability of Frame CTs. If the Commission desires
 a limited refresh of CONE, it could make a simple adjustment using TEF-supported units but
 without changing the reference technology or levelization method.
 The load forecast should incorporate SB 6 criteria for large loads (per P. 58480 and P. 58481),
 as well as other adjustments to reflect (i) the different purposes of the forecast, and (ii)
 ERCOT's expectations for transmission development and the batch study process. Given the
 uncertainty, it could be helpful for ERCOT to run multiple sensitivities for load growth.
 The generation in the December 2025 CDR Report does not accurately capture the resource
 mix. There are assumptions around plant retirements and new capacity that should be revisited.
 ERCOT's proposed magnitude values are too low and the continued reduction in expected
 magnitude despite load growth suggests that there are issues with the methodology. The
 magnitude should reflect the actual curtailment toolkit available to transmission and
 distribution providers during extreme events with high demand.
 Equal weighting of historical weather years gives undue weight to extremely unlikely 1-in-100
 events like Winter Storm Uri. Extreme outlier events should be weighted to correspond with
 their actual likelihood of occurrence to avoid low-probability events driving the study' s results.
 The Commission should reject ERCOT' s recommendation to reduce the effectiveness of the
 weatherization rule when recent experience supports the opposite conclusion.
 ERCOT's modeling may double-count generation outages by combining standard thermal and
 weather-related outages. More transparency into ERCOT' s calculations is necessary.
